frase_gancho.texto: A turquoise mirror that protected the warrior’s back.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the turquoise mosaic we move on to another mosaic, this one of shell: a breastplate made from plates of the sea, which speaks of trade routes that were longer still.

guion_corto.texto: This disc, a little over thirty centimeters across, is a tezcacuitlapilli, the “mirror of the back.” It was tied at the waist, over the back, and it was a mark of rank for chiefs. Look at how it is made: a base of wood and stone covered with thousands of tiny pieces of turquoise, with details of pyrite, shell and jet, forming fire serpents around a sunken center that once shone like a mirror. It is the same jewel that the Atlantean figure wears on its back, here in its most precious version. And the turquoise may have traveled from very far away: it has been proposed that it came from more than two thousand kilometers away.

guion_largo.texto:
Let’s start with the name, which explains the piece. Tezcacuitlapilli is formed from tezcatl, “mirror,” and cuitlapilli, “tail”: the mirror-tail, or mirror of the back. Important warriors and priests tied it at the waist, at the level of the lower back, with a leather belt. It is the same disc that the Atlantean figure wears on its back, carved in stone; the one in front of you is the luxury version, made in earnest with precious stones.

It is made up of thousands of tesserae, the tiny pieces of a mosaic, cut one by one from green and blue turquoise and glued with resin. Among them are thin plates of pyrite, red shell and jet that give it contrast. The central design is four fire serpents, xiuhcóatl, coiled around a hollow that must originally have shone, as if it were a small mirror. Making it took weeks of patient work, tessera by tessera.

Turquoise was the stone of fire. In Nahuatl, xihuitl means turquoise, year, grass and comet all at once; that is why Xiuhtecuhtli, the Old God of Fire whom you saw in the previous halls, is the “Lord of Turquoise,” and the xiuhcóatl, the fire serpent, is his weapon. The Mexica will say that Huitzilopochtli killed [Coyolxauhqui](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui) with a xiuhcóatl. In the Mexica Hall you will see that fire serpent once more, turned into a divine weapon.

Where did so much turquoise come from? Some propose that a good part of what reached Mesoamerica was mined far to the north, in what is now the southwestern United States, more than two thousand kilometers from Tula. If so, this jewel traveled enormous roads, perhaps passing through the region you will see in the North Hall, and in exchange for it, quetzal feathers, cacao and other products of the south traveled in the opposite direction. It is a hypothesis, but it sums up well how the ancient world worked: nothing was isolated.

Now let’s talk about mirrors. Those of Mesoamerica were not made of glass and silver: they were made of polished obsidian, pyrite or slate, and they were used for seeing, but above all for divining. An obsidian mirror of Mexica origin ended up in sixteenth-century England, in the hands of the astrologer John Dee, and today it is in the British Museum. And remember the god Tezcatlipoca, whose name means “Smoking Mirror”: he was the god who saw everything, the one who knew what was in the heart of every person.

With this we come to the legend you began to learn about in the mural at the entrance. According to the chronicles, written after the Conquest, Tezcatlipoca visited Quetzalcóatl, the priest-king of Tula, and showed him a mirror. Quetzalcóatl saw in it an old, tired, deformed face, and he was ashamed. With that deception the king’s downfall began. A mirror, then, was the weapon with which one god defeated another. Imagine what it could have meant to someone who carried one on his back.

It has also been said that the shine of these discs dazzled enemies, and that it protected the back from spiritual harm. The two explanations do not contradict each other. What is certain is that a man with a shining disc on his back seemed to carry the Sun with him, and that this reflection marked him as someone who held power over others.

Look at the disc slowly, searching for the finest points: every tiny tessera is a decision. And think that, as the warrior walked across the plaza, the midday light struck sparks from those thousands of blue fragments. No one would see him pass without noticing.

texto: Find the four fire serpents that coil around the center
Notice the range of colors in the turquoise, from green to blue
Imagine this disc on the back of the Atlantean figure, flashing in the sun

texto.Material: Wood with mosaic of turquoise, malachite, mother-of-pearl shell, and pyrite
texto.Origin: Tula, Hidalgo (Palacio Quemado, in an offering together with the shell breastplate)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ancient mirrors of Mexico were only decorations.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were objects of power: they were used for divining, for displaying rank and, according to the myths, even for deceiving a god.
